title: Worst case scenario; Jail suicide shows what can go wrong when mental health cases mishandled, inquest told
article: Cleve "Cas" Geddes' suicide in the Ottawa jail could make other families dealing with mental illness afraid to call police for help, the lawyer representing the Geddes family warned Monday at a coroner's inquest.
Geddes hanged himself in jail, eight days after being arrested by OPP officers investigating a complaint made by his father, Donald Denning, that Cleve had threatened him.

"I'm concerned that if some members of the community, hearing Mr. Denning's story and knowing that his son was arrested and eight days later ended up dead, they might be even more concerned," lawyer Paul Champ said.

"What are we going to tell other parents of schizophrenic children to do?" Champ quoted from the OPP's own training material - Not Just Another Arrest - while questioning a panel of OPP experts on how the force deals with mentally ill people.

Geddes, 29, suffered from paranoid schizophrenia and had a long history of uttering threats, but had never been violent and had no criminal record except for a 10-yearold suspended sentence that saw him admitted to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto.
Geddes was arrested for threatening and assaulting the OPP officers who investigated Denning's complaint.
The judge ordered he be sent to a psychiatric hospital for a mental health assessment, but because there were no beds available, he ended up at the Ottawa Carleton Detention Centre.
He spent eight days there, frequently on suicide watch and in segregation, before his death.
The inquest, under presiding coroner Dr. Michael B.
Wilson, is trying to determine what went wrong during Geddes'arrest, at his court appearance and at the jail.
On Monday, the jury heard testimony from the arresting officer and a four-member police panel that testified about the resources, policy and training surrounding mental-health cases.

Like other police forces, the number of OPP arrests involving mentally ill people has skyrocketed from 8,600 cases in 2007 to 12,400 in 2013, said Lisa Longworth, a civilian OPP employee who helped develop its mental-health strategy.

Though nearly 60 per cent of the OPP's detachments have developed a strategy for dealing with mental-health cases - working with local health-care and mental-health agencies, for example - that strategy can be very different in different parts of the province.
"It's going to look very different in downtown Toronto than it will in Killaloe," she said.
The Killaloe detachment normally has five officers on duty to cover 7,500 square kilometres across two counties, each with different hospitals and mental-health agencies.
Another impediment are privacy laws that can prevent health-care providers from sharing information with police or police officers from communicating with an arrested person's family.
Earlier in the day, supporter of Geddes and other inmates who've died by suicide rallied at the Canadian Tribute to Human Rights.
"Who would want to call the police knowing this could happen?" Geddes sister, Sigrid, said outside the inquest.
"Who would trust them?" She said her brother had a big heart and was "a golden boy" until his illness took hold.
"He was so sad and angry that he was sick," she said.
"We're hoping that Cas's suffering will put pressure on the government to make changes for people with mental health issues."
The inquest continues Tuesday.
